extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and readers of theatre/acting; general educated public interested in dramatic art
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and interpretive standards for judging 19th‑century stage acting, contrasting Romantic and Classic schools and illustrating qualities that made Edwin Forrest effective (e.g., sincerity, unity of conception, physical realism, imaginative portraiture). Useful for theatre criticism, actor training, and historical assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank of a work of art
rubrics_metrics.description: The rank of any work of art is determined by the ideal expressed in it, and the accuracy of its expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a performance by (1) identifying the artistic ideal it embodies and (2) judging how accurately and consistently that ideal is realized. Examples: Kemble's ideal = authority; Kean's = retribution; Cooke's = skepticism. A performance should be assessed on both conception and fidelity of execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic ideal / individuality of the actor
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor's central ideal (personal temperament and moral/intellectual bent) shapes effectiveness; Forrest exemplified a democratic, affirmative, and sincere ideal—unshackled individuality allied with moral elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging, note whether the actor's conception springs from a coherent personal ideal (e.g., universal manhood, heroism, sincerity) and whether that ideal illuminates a variety of rôles (Rolla, Tell, Spartacus, Damon, Brutus, Othello, Lear). Originality and nationality (distinctly American) are praised when they produce a consistent, inspiring persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Romantic and Classic schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasted styles: the Romantic (sensational/natural, characters of physical and mental realism) and the Classic (reflective/artistic, characters of imaginative portraiture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a performance by which school it aligns with, and evaluate on the school's own terms. The Romantic is impulsive, mimetic, and full of force; the Classic is self-controlled, studied, and expressive via pose and nuance. The best actors may combine elements of both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic / sensational acting (characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensational acting springs from strong and sincere impulses, is imitative or reproductive, projects things as they exist in reality, and exhibits physical and nervous force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for spontaneity, impetuosity, abandon, abrupt force, and visceral physical expression. It thrills broad, unsophisticated audiences; it can be expensive of bodily exertion and centered in the nervous centres of the body. Appropriate where subject/situation demand vivid sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classic / artistic acting (characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic acting originates in the creative mind, is self-controlled, economical of exertion, founded on thought and imagination, and relies on studied poses, attitudes, and refined measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of systematic study, mental mastery, and subtlety: consistency of conception, controlled gestures, and an intelligible intellectual shaping of feeling. Suited to cultivated audiences; effectiveness measured by refinement and expressive economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and acceptable use of melodrama
rubrics_metrics.description: Melodramatic action is physical rather than mental, emphasizing situations over revelation of character; pantomimic passion is melodramatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) melodrama as necessary physical movement to serve the plot (legitimate) and (b) melodrama as vulgar exaggeration and hollow sensationalism (vice). An actor may produce melodramatic effects when the subject requires them, but must avoid artifices that disregard congruity and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling passed through thought (emotion via intellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: True art is 'feeling passed through thought and fixed in form': emotion should be intellectualized and then allowed to run automatic through the nerves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether an actor has disciplined emotion by thought so that expression becomes natural and effortless. Positive indicator: controlled spontaneity. Anti-pattern: continued conscious volition in performance producing muscular friction and laboriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of excessive volition / muscular expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive conscious volition in play leads to a muscular friction and organic expense that make performance repulsive to sensitive observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark as a defect when an actor's brain continues to micromanage expression onstage (visible strain, overwrought physicality). Strong actors permit the brain to hand work to automatic nerves after intellectual formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural conversational delivery versus elocutionary mannerism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer straightforward truth and varied, hearty inflection of nature to mouthing formality, torpid noisiness, strained monotony, and forced cadences of routine theatrical delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value speech that resembles living utterance—changes, abruptness, conversational vivacity—over declamatory, mechanical elocution. Forrest exemplified substitution of natural inflection for elocutionary mannerism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and consistency of role conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete image of the character—carriage, walk, attitudes, gesture style, physiognomy, tone and habit of voice—should be fashioned and imprinted so as to produce unity of design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an actor has a deeply formed, consistently manifested conception across all details; assess continuity of manner, gesture, and vocal habit in sustaining an integrated portrait (compared to a master painter's unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective by-play and nuanced physical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtle by-play—small physical choices and timing—can produce startling power and convey contending emotions (e.g., the half-kneel in Rolla).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to small, truthful actions that reveal inner emotion (hesitations, half-movements, micro-expressions). These details often have greater effect than grand declamation when authentically motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, earnestness, and moral congruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and earnestness, and careful maintenance of congruity in representation, are central virtues; the actor should avoid hollow artificiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate the performance's honesty: is the feeling genuine and sustained, and does the representation cohere morally and aesthetically? Forrest praised for being 'always sincere, always earnest, always careful of the sustained congruity of his representation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical embodiment and presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Physique, carriage, vocal power, and an imposing physical presence contribute materially to dramatic effect (e.g., Forrest's deep square chest, broad shoulders, columnar neck, and sonorous voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether physical attributes and their controlled use (posture, movement, voice color) support and enhance the character; physical gifts may amplify the actor's ideal and emotional expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal appropriate to audience (cultivated Few vs unsophisticated Many)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different styles address different audiences: Classic refinements delight the cultivated Few, Romantic sensationalism thrills the unsophisticated Many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, consider intended audience and whether the actor's style fits that audience's expectations and capacities. Neither style is intrinsically superior; effectiveness depends on congruity with aims and spectatorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality from experience vs servile imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: An original actor often develops by direct experience and self-education, rather than by servile imitation of imported models; such originality yields a distinctive national or individual stamp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value novelty and individuality that arise from personal observation and lived feeling. Forrest's lack of early models forced him to shape his own resources, producing a fresh, national style. Penalize mere imitation and lifeless reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as poetic moral revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should function as poetry that reveals the moral ingredients of man, enlarged and glorified; spectators often prefer to be moved rather than to judge pedantically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tragic performance for its capacity to elevate moral sentiment and to move audiences empathetically. Beware critics who privilege detached fastidiousness over the play's moral and emotional purpose.
